Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Governor of South Carolina|Governor]] [[Mark Sanford]] won re-election against [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[South Carolina Senate|State Senator]] [[Tommy Moore (politician)|Tommy Moore]], becoming only the third Republican governor in South Carolina to win a second term ([[Robert Kingston Scott]] and [[Carroll A. Campbell Jr.]] were the others). Sanford started the campaign with a double-digit edge over Moore, and he maintained that lead to election day. During the campaign, Sanford's approval rating averaged in the mid-fifties.{{cite web |url=http://www.surveyusa.com/client/PollTrack.aspx?g=79bc576e-2f1d-4cec-a2b4-94aecce55b09 |title=Do you approve or disapprove of the job Mark Sanford is doing as Governor? |publisher=SurveyUSA}} In Sanford's re-election victory, he garnered 22% of the African American vote. ==Democratic primary== [[Tommy Moore (politician)|Tommy Moore]], a [[South Carolina Senate|state senator]] from western South Carolina, emerged with [[Florence, South Carolina|Florence]] Mayor Frank Willis as the major candidates in the Democratic [[Partisan primary|primary election]] for governor. Rumors circulated that Superintendent of Education and former [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] candidate [[Inez Tenenbaum]] might enter the race, but she ultimately chose not to run for governor nor seek re-election to her position. [[Kenneth Lamar Holland|Kenneth Holland]], a former [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] from [[South Carolina's 5th congressional district|the 5th congressional district]], briefly entered the race, but dropped out a month later after failing to raise enough financial contributions. Moore and Willis traded barbs over campaign contributions made by Willis and his wife to prominent Republicans, including President [[George W. Bush]] and Senator [[Lindsey Graham]]. Attorney C. Dennis Aughtry entered the campaign at the eleventh hour and floated the idea of legalizing casinos statewide to raise money for public schools. Moore garnered more than 50% of the vote in the Democratic primary held on June 13 and thus avoided a [[Two-round system|runoff election]]. {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{cite web |title=South Carolina Election Returns - June 13, 2006 Democratic Primary - Official Results |url=http://www.scvotes.org/files/06primaryOfficial/DemocratStatewide.pdf |publisher=South Carolina State Election Commission |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150330064118/http://www.scvotes.org/files/06primaryOfficial/DemocratStatewide.pdf |archive-date=March 30, 2015 |url-status=dead}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Tommy Moore | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 88,092 | percentage = 63.68 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Frank Willis | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 42,317 | percentage = 30.59 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = C. Dennis Aughtry | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 7,934 | percentage = 5.74 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 138,343 | percentage = 100 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== [[File:2006 South Carolina governor Republican primary.svg|thumb|230px|Primary results by county: {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#ed8783|Sanford}} |{{legend|#ed8783|50–60%}} |{{legend|#e55651|60–70%}} |{{legend|#d02923|70–80%}} |{{legend|#b00600|80–90%}} }} {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#c88fe4|Lovelace}} |{{legend|#c88fe4|50–60%}} |{{legend|#b368d9|60–70%}} }} ]] Portending a sign of trouble, incumbent [[Governor of South Carolina|Governor]] [[Mark Sanford]] faced a [[primary challenge]] from [[Oscar Lovelace]], a [[physician]] from the [[Midlands, South Carolina|Midlands]]. When former Governor [[David Beasley]] ran for [[South Carolina gubernatorial election, 1998|re-election in 1998]], he faced a primary challenge and went on to lose the general election to [[Jim Hodges]]. Sanford's veto of a heart center for [[Lexington County, South Carolina|Lexington County]] and theatrics such as bringing pigs to the [[South Carolina Statehouse|Statehouse]] to show his displeasure of [[pork barrel]] spending by the [[South Carolina General Assembly|General Assembly]] angered and annoyed many Republicans. However, Sanford's strategy of avoiding Lovelace and refusal to debate worked as the governor scored a decisive victory in the primary on June 13. {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results{{cite web |title=South Carolina Election Returns - June 13, 2006 Republican Primary - Official Results |url=https://www.scvotes.gov/files/06primaryOfficial/RepublicanStatewide.pdf |publisher=South Carolina State Election Commission |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802021021/https://www.scvotes.gov/files/06primaryOfficial/RepublicanStatewide.pdf |archive-date=August 2, 2022 |url-status=dead}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Mark Sanford (incumbent) | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 160,238 | percentage = 64.80 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Oscar Lovelace | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 87,043 | percentage = 35.20 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 247,281 | percentage = 100 }} {{Election box end}} ==Campaign== Governor Mark Sanford proposed three major issues in his campaign for re-election, chief among them being the restructuring of state government. He wanted to reduce the number of statewide elected officials from nine to three and eliminate the state's Budget and Control Board. The governor insisted that these measures would reduce the number of redundant positions and make state government both more efficient and less costly. Sanford's three major issues for the campaign were: *Restructuring state government *[[School choice]] through tuition tax credits *[[Tax cuts]] and spending restraint State Senator Tommy Moore ran as a good manager of state government. He held socially conservative and fiscally moderate positions, which put him squarely at odds with the [[Libertarianism|libertarian]] incumbent. Moore disagreed with what he believed was Sanford's condescending and combative approach of dealing with the General Assembly. The senator also believed that Sanford lacked leadership skills, and that lack of leadership had brought South Carolina to a standstill over the past four years in his view. The main policy proposals that he developed were: *A rural infrastructure bank to help undeveloped counties *A governor's office that actively recruits new businesses to the state *A 30-cent tax increase on cigarettes to offset small business tax credits for employee health insurance On July 7, several weeks after the primary election, [[Lexington County, South Carolina|Lexington County]] [[South Carolina Senate|State Senator]] [[Jake Knotts]] launched a last-minute effort to place his name on the ballot as a petition candidate for governor. He had feuded with Governor Sanford over a number of issues, including the heart center for Lexington County, and supported Lovelace in the Republican primary. In order to be on the ballot in November, Knotts needed to collect 10,000 signatures of registered voters by July 17, which he failed to do. Knotts's political consultant publicly stated that he could not have raised enough money to have run a successful candidacy. There were two trains of thought on the effects of a candidacy by Knotts. It was generally believed that had Knotts entered the race, it would have split the Republican vote and helped elect Tommy Moore. However, because those who supported Knotts went on to support Moore, it was also argued that a Knotts candidacy would have in fact deprived Moore of both votes and money. === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- !
